title: Fuzzing in the GenAI Era — Leonard Tang, Haize Labs

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is evaluation design, testing methodology, LLM judges, and benchmarking for GenAI systems. The evaluation methodology is cross-domain, with case studies in financial services and customer-support voice agents. The talk addresses pre-deployment evaluation and testing to find corner cases before production release. Requires familiarity with LLM applications and basic evaluation concepts, with optional RL knowledge. A conference presentation at AI Engineer by Leonard Tang, founder and CEO of Haize Labs. All evidence anchors are directly stated in the transcript with said_in_transcript grade.

summary: Leonard Tang frames Haize Labs as a QA/eval company focused on validating subjective, unstructured LLM outputs. The 'last mile problem' is that GenAI apps are easy to prototype but achieving enterprise-grade reliability remains unsolved. The root cause is GenAI 'brittleness' (Lipschitz discontinuity) — syntactically or semantically similar inputs yield wildly divergent outputs, exemplified by Air Canada, Character AI, and Chevy incidents. Standard evaluation fails in two ways: coverage (static datasets cannot densely cover input space) and quality measurement (translating subjective SME criteria into quantitative metrics is unsolved; existing tools all have quirks). Haize's 'hazing' approach iteratively simulates stimuli, judges outputs, and guides search to find corner cases. For judging, LLM-as-judge alone fails due to hallucination, instability, miscalibration, and biases. Their 'scaling judge time compute' spans two approaches: (1) structured agent-based judges via the Verdict library, using scalable oversight primitives (debate, self-verification, ensembling) — a GPT-4o mini backbone with self-verified debate ensemble beats o1, o3 mini, GPT-4, and 3.5 Sonnet on expert QA verification at less than a third of cost and latency; (2) RL tuning from scratch via GRPO, inspired by DeepSeek's SPCT (self-principled critique tuning), producing instance-specific rubrics and critiques — a 1.7B parameter model achieves 80.7% on reward bench, matching Claude 3 Opus and GPT-4 mini. For stimuli generation, fuzzing in AI is more structured and optimization-driven than classical security, since brute-force search over natural language is intractable. Haize treats it as discrete optimization, using gradient-based methods, tree search/MCTS, latent space search, and DSPy to find inputs that minimize judge scores. Case studies include hazing a major Hungarian bank's loan calculation AI (finding prompt injections and corner cases against an 18-line code of conduct), a F500 bank's outbound debt collection voice agents (adding audio perturbations; what took internal teams 3 months took the platform 5 minutes), and a voice agent company achieving 38% increase in ground truth human agreement using Verdict's rubric fanout architecture.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Haize's Mission
sections.summary: Tang introduces Haize Labs as working on validating, verifying, auditing, and steering subjective LLM outputs. Despite being in the AI security track, he positions them as a QA/eval/property-based testing ('hazing') company.

sections.title: The Last Mile Problem in AI
sections.summary: Explains that while GenAI apps are easy to make demo-ready, achieving enterprise-grade reliability remains unsolved. Large-scale simulation, optimization, and search before deployment is Haize's approach to pressure-testing systems.

sections.title: Brittleness of GenAI Applications
sections.summary: Defines brittleness as Lipschitz discontinuity: slightly varied inputs producing wildly different outputs. Distinguishes this from nondeterminism, which is manageable at temperature zero. Cites Air Canada, Character AI, and Chevy truck incidents as manifestations.

sections.title: Inadequacy of Standard Evaluation Methods
sections.summary: Standard evals fail in two primary senses: insufficient coverage (static datasets can't densely cover input space) and difficulty of quality measurement (translating subjective SME criteria into quantitative metrics remains unsolved; existing tools all have quirks).

sections.title: Hazing: Simulating the Last Mile
sections.summary: Describes hazing in the abstract: simulate large-scale stimuli, judge and score outputs, use signals to guide next search round iteratively until bugs are found or budget is exhausted.

sections.title: LLM-as-Judge Limitations and Scaling Judge Time Compute
sections.summary: LLM-as-judge fails due to hallucination, instability, miscalibration, and biases. Haize's philosophy is 'scaling judge time compute,' ranging from training reasoning models from scratch to using structured agent-based judges via the Verdict library with scalable oversight primitives.

sections.title: Verdict Benchmark Results
sections.summary: Presents benchmarks showing Verdict (powered by GPT-4o mini with self-verified debate ensemble architecture) beats o1, o3 mini, GPT-4, and 3.5 Sonnet on expert QA verification at less than a third of cost and latency, demonstrating the value of carefully chosen priors in agent-based judge design.

sections.title: RL-Tuned Judges via GRPO and SPCT
sections.summary: Describes the second approach to scaling judge compute: training models from scratch via GRPO, inspired by DeepSeek's SPCT (self-principled critique tuning). SPCT proposes instance-specific criteria (like unit tests per data point) and critiques against them. A 1.7B parameter GRPO-trained model achieves 80.7% on reward bench, matching Claude 3 Opus and GPT-4 mini, with similar results for a 600M model — demonstrating that small models with more targeted compute can match frontier judges.

sections.title: Fuzzing vs. Adversarial Testing and Stimuli Generation
sections.summary: Distinguishes fuzzing (testing with reasonable in-distribution input variants) from adversarial testing (emulating prompt injection and jailbreak attempts). AI fuzzing is far more structured and optimization-driven than classical security fuzzing because brute-force search over natural language is intractable (128K token vocabulary). Haize treats stimuli generation as discrete optimization, minimizing judge scores via gradient-based methods, tree search/MCTS, latent space search, and DSPy.

sections.title: Case Studies: Hungarian Bank, F500 Voice Agents, and Voice Agent Eval Scaling
sections.summary: Three case studies: (1) Hazing Hungary's largest bank's loan calculation AI against an 18-line code of conduct, discovering prompt injections, jailbreaks, and unexpected corner cases that were then patched for production. (2) A F500 bank's outbound debt collection voice agents — adding audio perturbations (background noise, static, frequency changes); what took internal ops teams 3 months took the platform 5 minutes. (3) A voice agent company achieving 38% increase in ground truth human agreement using Verdict's rubric fanout architecture (propose criteria, critique, self-verify, aggregate).

sections.title: Q&A and Closing
sections.summary: Tang notes Haize is aggressively hiring, facing insurmountable enterprise demand as a four-person team based in New York. In Q&A, he confirms hazing supports single-turn, multi-turn, persistent conversations, and all modalities including voice.
